new_statements.quote: El acento en el idioma Poqomchi' es fijo y cae en la última sílaba, excepto en algunas palabras que provienen del español que siguen manteniendo su acento (71). Por la posición fija del acento no se escribe ortográficamente. [ex. 70: [kamaníkʰ] trabajo, [haʔlak'ún] bebé, [ʔih má:m] nieto, [k'aník'] lombriz de estómago, [perepíkʰ] plano; ex. 71: [kánte:la] candela, [níspero] níspero, [rámnaʰ] su alma] ... 72) Las palabras provenientes del idioma Nawatl también tienen acento prosódico en la última sílaba. [čikiwítʰ] canasto, [tinamít] pueblo
new_statements.translation: Stress in the Poqomchi' language is fixed and falls on the last syllable, except in some words that come from Spanish, which keep their own stress (71). Because of the fixed position of stress it is not written orthographically. ... 72) Words coming from Nawatl also have prosodic stress on the last syllable.
new_statements.citation: Mó Isém, Romelia (2006). Fonología y morfología del Poqomchi' Occidental. Tesis de licenciatura en Lingüística, Universidad Rafael Landívar, Facultad de Humanidades, Departamento de Letras y Filosofía, Guatemala de la Asunción, octubre de 2006 (asesora: Nora C. England).
new_statements.locator: Capítulo Fonología, §4 'Acento', p. 44 (PDF p. 58); loan-stress remarks §1.4 'Acento y prolongaciones vocálicas', pp. 56-57
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (375 pp. extracted text of PDF p. 58 (printed p. 44) and the page render both show section '4 Acento' with the prose exactly as quoted: 'El acento en el idioma Poqomchi' es fijo y cae en la última sílaba, excepto en algunas palabras que provienen del español que siguen manteniendo su acento (71). Por la posición fija del acento no se escribe ortográficamente.' and '72) Las palabras provenientes del idioma Nawatl también tienen acento prosódico en la última sílaba.' The only differences are in the bracketed example forms, which the reader IPA-normalised from the PDF's broken-font glyphs (source text layer/render: [kamaníkH], [ha0lak'ún], [0ih má:m], [perepíkH], [CikiwítH]; report: [ka…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of every native word, regardless of syllable weight or vowel length (Weichel 2006:25 adds that the correlate is higher pitch, secondarily loudness, and that length and stress are independent). Spanish loans keep their Spanish stress position (with the stressed vowel lengthened on adaptation); Nahuatl loans are final-stressed like native words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Mó Isém 2006 or Weichel 2006. Stoll 1888:19 (Tactic dialect) notes that in the sentence the final word's ultima is most prominent while possessive prefixes, prepositions and the demonstrative i are unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loanwords retain Spanish stress (Mó Isém ex. 71 [kánte:la], [níspero], [rámnaʰ]; Weichel exx. 2.64-2.67 [méša] 'table', [wákaš] 'cow', [šawéla] 'Isabelle', [máŋka] 'mango'). Weichel 2006:26-27: one native exception /čaxári/ 'What?' (San Cristóbal dialect only), explained as a fossilised compound of /čih xarík/; irregularly stressed forms are marked in her transcriptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('cae en la última sílaba' of the word; Weichel: 'Word stress.. falls almost exclusively on the last syllable in a word'). Weichel §2.4 phonetic transcriptions are of citation forms elicited in San Cristóbal Verapaz. Both sources describe the western dialect (San Cristóbal Verapaz, Santa Cruz Verapaz, Belejú/Chicamán).
new_statements.identity_note: poqo1256 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO 639-3 code [pob] 'Western Pokomchí', merged into Poqomchi' [poh] (Glottolog poqo1254) by ISO CR 2008-058 (effective 2009-01-16; file). Both quoted sources describe exactly this western dialect (San Cristóbal Verapaz, Santa Cruz Verapaz, Belejú/Chicamán): Mó Isém 2006 is titled 'Poqomchi' Occidental' and Weichel 2006 'Western Pokomchi'' (San Cristóbal Verapaz fieldwork). The catalog record for poqo1254 already rests on the same Mó Isém 2006:44 quotation, so this entry duplicates poqo1254 rather than adding an independent language; Stoll 1888 (Tactic) is the central/eastern dialect.

new_statements.quote: p. 25: "The most prominent phonetic correlate of stress is pitch, as stressed syllables are articulated with a higher pitch than unstressed syllables. They also tend to be articulated at a higher volume. Word stress is generally predictable in Pokomchi', as it falls almost exclusively on the last syllable in a word, regardless of the syllable weight of this syllable" [exx. 2.58-2.63]. p. 26: "There are few exceptions to this, most of which are borrowings from Spanish" [2.64-2.67 mesa, wakas, sawela, manka keep Spanish stress]. fn. 6, p. 20: "The phonetic correlate of word stress is pitch, and vowel length and word stress are independent."

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Mó Isém 2006 statement (fixed final). Adds: stress is weight-insensitive, pitch is its main correlate, length and stress are independent, one native lexical exception besides Spanish loans. Fieldwork San Cristóbal Verapaz 2004 (western dialect), so it is about this variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the last syllable of the word regardless of syllable weight; its main phonetic cue is higher pitch (and loudness); vowel length is phonemic and independent of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loans keep their Spanish stress ([mesa] 'table', [wakas] 'cow', [sawela] 'Isabelle', [manka] 'mango'); one native exception /caxari/ 'What?' (San Cristóbal dialect only), explained on pp. 26-27 as a fossilised phrase (/cih xarik/ ~ /ca:x wo' xarik/) that preserved the stress of /caxar/. Irregular stress is marked in the thesis's transcriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: poqo1256 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry for retired ISO [pob] 'Western Pokomchi' (San Cristóbal Verapaz, Santa Cruz Verapaz, Belejú/Chicamán), merged into Poqomchi' [poh] = poqo1254 by ISO CR 2008-058 (effective 2009-01-16). Mó Isém 2006 and Weichel 2006 describe exactly this western variety; Weichel's native exception /caxari/ is San Cristóbal only. Stoll 1888 describes the Tactic variety (central/eastern). The unopened ALMG grammar is a pan-dialect normative grammar.

new_statements.translation: p. 44: "Stress in the Poqomchi' language is fixed and falls on the last syllable, except in some words that come from Spanish, which keep their [original] stress (71). Because of the fixed position of the stress it is not written in the orthography." (72) "Words that come from the Nawatl language also have prosodic stress on the last syllable."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Fixed word stress on the final syllable; not written because it is predictable.
new_statements.exceptions: Some Spanish loans keep Spanish stress ([kánte:la], [níspero], [rámnaʰ]); §1.4 p. 56 adds that loans stressed on the last or penultimate syllable lengthen that vowel when adapted (asukaar, kotoon, kapeew, waasa, meexah..). Nahuatl loans take final stress.

sources.quote: p. 25: "The most prominent phonetic correlate of stress is pitch, as stressed syllables are articulated with a higher pitch than unstressed syllables. They also tend to be articulated at a higher volume. Word stress is generally predictable in Pokomchi', as it falls almost exclusively on the last syllable in a word, regardless of the syllable weight of this syllable" [exx. 2.58-2.63]. p. 26: "There are few exceptions to this, most of which are borrowings from Spanish" [2.64-2.67 mesa, wakas, sawela, manka keep Spanish stress]. fn. 6, p. 20: "The phonetic correlate of word stress is pitch, and vowel length and word stress are independent."
sources.note: §2.4 'Stress', pp. 25-27 (PDF pp. 41-43; renders weichel2006_p41-42-041/): 'Word stress is generally predictable in Pokomchi', as it falls almost exclusively on the last syllable in a word, regardless of the syllable weight of this syllable'; correlate is pitch (also volume); few exceptions, mostly Spanish loans ([mésa], [wákaš], [šawéla], [máŋka]); one native exception /čaxári/ 'What?' (San Cristóbal only), explained as a fossilised phrase. Fn. 6 p. 20: vowel length and word stress are independent. Copy held under poqo1254 was re-downloaded from uregina.scholaris.

sources.note: 'Betonung', p. 19: 'Im Pokonchí ist der Wortaccent viel bestimmter ausgebildet als im Ixil, und zwar ist fast stets die Ultima die Trägerin des Accentes'; also in the sentence the ultima is always stressed and each major word carries an accent on its ultima; possessive prefixes, prepositions and demonstrative i are unstressed ('tonlos'). Summary: 'Der Accent fällt vorwiegend auf die Ultima.' Other dialect (Tactic), archive.org scanned only.
